question.context: A command and control behavior was blocked on host `vnevado-win10r`, which indicated an active infection by malware that could replicate and receive commands from remote attackers. This malware was active, and precautionary measures should be taken to check for residual signs of infection. The process involved had the ID 1332 and ran the command `curl http://vectorsandarrows.com`.
question.question: What is the IP address associated with the Manatee Tempest activity group detected in this security incident?
solution: The account with SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522` was involved in a Command and Control behavior that was blocked.
The cybercriminal group known as Manatee Tempest, which is associated with the IP address `198.43.121.209`, was active during the incident.

Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

question.context: A Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on a device at 2024-07-04 22:35:03.797541+00:00. Mimikatz is a tool used to harvest plaintext passwords, password hashes, smartcard PINs, and Kerberos tickets. The attacker might be leveraging this tool to harvest credentials to log into this or other devices on the network by impersonating a valid user. Several command line executions involving `mimikatz.exe` were observed, along with connected mimikatz-related files like `mimidrv.sys`, `mimispool.dll`, and `mimilove.exe`. More information can be found in the Mimikatz tool profile Threat Analytics report and the Actor profile: Storm-0875 Threat Analytics report provided by Microsoft.

('2024-06-20 09:40:00.646871+00:00', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

question.context: A possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected on the host `vnevado-win10s` involving user with username `dp5hn`. The PRT is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication used to enable single sign-on (SSO) across applications on supported devices, and attackers attempting to access this resource could be aiming for lateral movement or credential theft. The attempt was carried out by the process `browsercore.exe` as observed from the process ID `2676`.
question.question: Related to this alert, there was an active malware detected subsequently. Can you identify the name of the malware file detected on the machine?

question.context: There was a detection of unknown malware being active in the environment, which was stopped by Windows Defender but it is recommended to further check the machine for signs of infection. Following that, there were multiple alerts indicating possible attempts to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) which is a key artifact used for Azure AD authentication. Additionally, we observed an alert where system recovery settings were tampered with, indicating that adversaries might be attempting to delete or disable built-in operating system data and recovery services. This could prevent recovery of a corrupted system and denie access to backups and recovery options. Various built-in Windows utilities can be exploited to disable or delete system recovery features, posing a risk to system integrity.
question.question: What is the name of the account involved in the system recovery setting tampering incident?
solution: An unknown malware was detected and was active on the host with AadDeviceId `4d8d23e9-a77d-4e33-9435-b8c457e57ca1`.
There was a possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) involving the process `browsercore.exe`.
The user with SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522` was involved in a potential attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT).
System recovery setting tampering was observed on the account named `dp5hn`.

question.context: A security incident involving the Manatee Tempest activity group was flagged, where the actor Manatee Tempest, known for its early malware campaigns like the Dridex banking trojan, has been active since June 2014. The group utilizes tactics such as drive-by downloads and FakeUpdates infections, facilitated by Mustard Tempest to gain initial access. Later, they use the BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. One of the events related to this incident involved a process running on the host `vnevado-win11t` using the command `curl http://vectorsandarrows.com`. The Process ID was 88.

question.context: On July 4th, 2024, a ransomware payload was remotely launched on device 'vnevado-win11t' with IP address '99.83.111.100'. Attackers might be attempting to encrypt content on this device, rendering it unusable to users. For more information, refer to the Threat Analytics report: Threat overview: Human-operated ransomware.
question.question: Related to this alert, there was a possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT). What is the file name of the process that was used in this attempt?
solution: A ransomware payload was remotely launched on an account with the name `dp5hn`.
A possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected, involving the process with the filename `browsercore.exe`.

A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

Validate the alert.
1. Check if the device owner or IT personnel had a legitimate reason to launch the command.
2. Look for recent signs of activity by the compromised user account or device and investigate them. Make sure to check other devices in your organization, as well as the original device associated with the compromised assets.
3. Review device timelines for suspicious activity that may have occurred around the time of the alert.
4. Look for unfamiliar processes. Check files for prevalence, their locations, and digital signatures.
5. Submit relevant files for deep analysis and review file behaviors.
6. Look for the presence of relevant artifacts on other devices. Identify commonalities and differences between potentially compromised devices.

B. Scope the incident. Find related devices, network addresses, and files in the incident graph.

C. Contain and mitigate the breach.
1. Stop suspicious processes, isolate affected systems, decommission compromised accounts or reset passwords, block IP addresses and URLs, and install security updates.
2. If you believe that the alert is a false positive:
     2.1 A user may have been suspended automatically. Revert the action by enabling the user account through the MDI portal or Active Directory.

question.context: A recent security incident involved multiple attempts to access a Primary Refresh Token (PRT) which is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on various devices. During the investigation, it was observed that a suspicious activity attempted to access PRT from the account associated with the user `tgs2z`, possibly moving laterally within the organization. The IP address involved in this incident was `107.224.99.179`, and one of the processes noted was `powershell.exe`. This investigation further revealed a Command and Control (C2) behavior that was blocked.
question.question: What was the URL blocked due to Command and Control (C2) behavior in this incident?
solution: There was a possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) using the process `browsercore.exe`.
The account `dp5hn` was associated with a possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT).
Command and Control behavior was detected and blocked for the URL `http://vectorsandarrows.com/`.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report on the Microsoft Security website.

question.context: During an investigation of a security incident, it was observed that 'CommandAndControl' malware was detected on the host `vnevado-win10r`, which might be an indication of an attacker attempting to move laterally from another network device. The process was initiated via the command `curl http://vectorsandarrows.com` with Process ID 1332. The incident is part of a larger campaign by the Manatee Tempest activity group, which is known for various cyber-attacks including the use of Cobalt Strike beacons for lateral movement and ransomware deployment.
question.question: As part of the Manatee Tempest activity group, what is the IP address associated with their activity in this incident?
solution: The 'CommandAndControl' malware was detected on a device. An attacker might be attempting to move laterally to this device from another device on the network. The associated user account has the SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522`.

Manatee Tempest, a Russia-based cybercriminal group active since June 2014, was identified. This group was responsible for the Dridex banking trojan and various other malvertising and infection methods. They have been observed partnering with Mustard Tempest to facilitate initial access. They use the IP address `198.43.121.209` for their activities.

  Description,

  OR LOWER(DisplayName) LIKE '%unknown malware%'

  OR LOWER(Entities) LIKE '%cmd.exe%'

The Primary Refresh Token is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on various platforms and is essential for single sign-on (SSO) across applications.

This execution was flagged on 2024-07-04 at 22:35:03.869406+00:00 for its intent to dump user credentials. Subsequently, there was a lateral movement attempt to the jump server `Vnevado-jump` on 2024-07-10 at 11:24:45.260113+00:00.

question.context: A security incident involving an attempt to access a Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected. The PRT is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on various devices, including Windows 10. The incident involved a device with HostName `vnevado-win10s` and AadDeviceId `f5b847aa-8712-4bf6-b4f7-ed6cd89e1505`, where the process `browsercore.exe` (ProcessId `2676` created at `2024-06-20T09:10:59.867384Z`) was running. Attackers may use this to move laterally within the organization.
question.question: Following this incident, 'CommandAndControl' malware was detected on another device during lateral movement. What is the AadDeviceId of this affected device?
solution: A possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected for the user with AadUserId `731adb71-b11c-4bbf-850b-57989b350e96`.
'CommandAndControl' malware was detected on the device with AadDeviceId `bc00e484-d0e5-4da4-9472-95568cccc07e`, indicating an attempt of lateral movement.

[('e34d562e-ef12-4c4e-9bc0-7c6ae357c015', '2024-06-20 09:00:03.183652+00:00', 'Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', 'Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', 'Medium', "Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures ('2024-06-20 09:40:00.348632+00:00', 'Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', 'Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', "Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

('2024-06-20 09:44:53.875951+00:00', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', ('2024-06-20 09:44:53.945494+00:00', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures question.context: A security incident regarding System recovery setting tampering and possible attempts to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was reported. Specifically, there was an attempt to disable system recovery features using `vssblatemp.exe` and `bcdedit` on the host `vnevado-win11u` with a user account having the SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522`. Notably, it included a potential access of PRTs, as mentioned in the Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report.
question.question: In relation to the malicious credential theft tool execution detected in this multi-stage incident, can you identify the file name of the tool that was executed?
solution: The system recovery settings tampering was attempted by the user with AadUserId `731adb71-b11c-4bbf-850b-57989b350e96`.
An attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected, associated with the process `browsercore.exe`.
Another attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected, originating from the IP address `107.224.99.179`.
A malicious credential theft tool `mimikatz.exe` was executed.

question.context: A security incident involving the Manatee Tempest activity group was reported. This Russia-based cybercriminal group, which has been active since June 2014, is known for malware campaigns including the Dridex banking trojan. They often gain initial access through methods such as drive-by downloads and malvertising, facilitated by their partnership with Mustard Tempest. As part of this security incident, a suspicious WMI process creation was observed on the machine `vnevado-win10r`, which might be an indicator of malware using WMI to spawn new processes and further infect the machine.
question.question: Can you provide the command line details of the suspicious WMI process observed on the machine?

Attackers might modify LSASS memory to bypass security mechanisms or circumvent legitimate checks. In the same incident, the device `vnevado-win10v` showed signs of the Mimikatz hacktool being detected.
question.question: What is the name of the credential theft tool detected on the device `vnevado-win10v`?
solution: The LSASS process memory was modified on host `vnevado-win10v`.
The Mimikatz credential theft tool, known as mimikatz.exe, was detected on the same host `vnevado-win10v`.

question.context: A security incident involving suspected tampering with system recovery settings using various commands and processes, including `vssblatemp.exe` to delete all volume shadow copies, was observed on device `vnevado-win11t` (AAD Device ID: `e5799261-6720-4297-961e-bd9ca4275033`). During the incident, the process `vssblatemp.exe` was executed with command: `vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all`. This is part of an adversarial attempt to prevent the recovery of corrupted systems by deleting built-in operating system data or turning off recovery services. The incident was detected on 2024-07-04. This tampering could deny access to available backups and recovery options, augmenting the effects of data destruction or data encryption.
question.question: Can you identify the executable file name of the process that attempted to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) as part of the related alerts?
solution: There was system recovery setting tampering by the Azure AD user with AadUserId `731adb71-b11c-4bbf-850b-57989b350e96`.
There was a possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) involving the process `browsercore.exe`.

question.context: A Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on a device. Mimikatz is a credential theft tool that can harvest plaintext passwords, password hashes, smartcard PINs, and Kerberos tickets. Attackers may use this tool to harvest credentials to log into this or other devices on the network by impersonating a valid user. The detection of Mimikatz is part of a broader security investigation. Additionally, there was later evidence of lateral movement to the jump server `Vnevado-jump` using PSExec.
question.question: A related alert indicated a possible compromised user account dropping ransomware-related files. Can you identify the name of the specific file associated with the ransomware activity?
solution: The Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on the device with AadDeviceId `4d8d23e9-a77d-4e33-9435-b8c457e57ca1`.
Lateral movement to the jump server occurred using PSExec to IP address `99.83.111.100`.
A compromised user account was observed dropping a ransomware-related file named `get-userprttoken.ps1` on several devices.

question.question: During this incident, what specific command line was observed that could indicate system recovery setting tampering on the device?
solution: There was suspicious 'GenRansom' behavior detected on the device with AadDeviceId `e5799261-6720-4297-961e-bd9ca4275033`.
Lateral movement using SMB remote file access was blocked for the user with SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522`.
System recovery setting tampering was observed with the process having ProcessId `4312`, created at `2024-06-20t09:10:48.0676225z`, and the command line `bcdedit /set recoveryenabled no`.

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

('2024-06-20 09:40:00.646871+00:00', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures question.context: A security incident indicates that a possible compromised user account was observed delivering ransomware-related files like `ponceau.7z`, `ponceau.7z.lockbit`, `earlap.doc`, and `earlap.doc.lockbit` on several devices. An attacker may have used this compromised account to move laterally across the network and infect devices with ransomware. Automated remediation actions may be taken to disable the compromised account.
question.question: As per the recent alert, what is the name of the file that shows the potentially compromised assets exhibiting ransomware-like behavior?
solution: A user account was observed dropping a ransomware-related file `syncretic.7z.lockbit` on several devices.
Potentially compromised assets are exhibiting ransomware-like behavior with a file named `unstreaming.xlsx`, impacting several devices.

The command line used to delete all file snapshots and shadow copies was:
vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all

question.context: During a potential ransomware incident, several suspicious file modifications were detected on a device. These modifications involved appending a known malicious extension, indicative of mass file encryption. The related files include `kiters.7z.lockbit`, `ponceau.7z.lockbit`, `unstreaming.xlsx.lockbit`, `earlap.doc.lockbit`, among others. Additionally, an IP address `99.83.111.100` and a host with an AadDeviceId `bc00e484-d0e5-4da4-9472-95568cccc07e` are associated with this alert.
question.question: In connection to the potential ransomware activity, it was found that all file backups were deleted. Can you determine the name of the process that executed this deletion?
solution: Possible ransomware activity has been detected involving the mass encryption of files indicated by a known malicious extension, associated with the account with SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522`.
File backups, such as file snapshots and shadow copies, were deleted via WMI or VSSAdmin using the process `vssblatemp.exe`, which is common during ransomware infections.

('2024-06-20 09:19:23.662799+00:00', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'High', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures ('2024-06-20 09:40:00.275880+00:00', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'High', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures question.context: A serious security incident involving the Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on a device. Mimikatz is known for harvesting plaintext passwords, password hashes, smartcard PINs, and Kerberos tickets. An attacker might use this tool to obtain credentials to log into this or other devices on the network by impersonating a valid user. The tool was executed with several different command lines indicating privilege escalation and credential theft attempts.
question.question: What was the command line of the process detected with the known credential theft tool execution?
solution: The attacker launched `mimikatz.exe` with the command line `privilege::debug sekurlsa::pth /user:fk8mq /ntlm:96def1a633fc6790124d5f8fe21cc72b /domain:vnevado.alpineskihouse.co /run:..\notepad.exe \vnevado-jump cmd.exe` at `2024-06-20t09:05:15.5627318z`, with Process ID `6600`.
A malicious credential theft tool execution was detected with the command line `conhost.exe 0xffffffff -forcev1` at `2024-06-20t08:59:42.8455252z`, with Process ID `7948`.

       ae.Title,
       ae.EntityType,
       ae.EvidenceRole,
       ae.ProcessCommandLine
FROM AlertEvidence ae
JOIN SecurityAlert sa
  ON ae.AlertId = sa.SystemAlertId
WHERE sa.AlertName = 'Malicious credential theft tool execution detected'
  AND ae.ProcessCommandLine IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY ae.AlertId, ae.ProcessCommandLine

FROM AlertEvidence 
LIMIT 50

question.context: A security incident involving the Manatee Tempest activity group was detected. This group is known for using drive-by downloads and other methods to gain initial access, followed by using malware tools for lateral movement. The incident started with a suspicious activity involving a URL `http://vectorsandarrows.com`, accessed from host `vnevado-win10r` with IP address `198.43.121.209` via a curl command. The ProcessId__CreatedTimeUtc__CommandLine is `1332__2024-06-20t09:10:52.7298237z__curl http://vectorsandarrows.com`.
question.question: What is the host name of the device where 'CommandAndControl' malware was detected during lateral movement?
solution: Manatee Tempest, a Russia-based cybercriminal group, was involved in the use of access broker Mustard Tempest to facilitate infections and lateral movement using BLISTER loader and Cobalt Strike beacons on various networks. The group used domain fronting for command-and-control of Cobalt Strike.
A suspicious account with SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522` was identified in the context of the Manatee Tempest group activities.
The 'CommandAndControl' malware was detected on the host `vnevado-win10s`, indicating an attempt at lateral movement within the network.

It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

('3f25b0c7-fcf6-aee6-7790-0b8e5ba10dd7', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', ('2829a21b-e106-56bf-60d9-14f53f63cb7f', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

question.context: A security incident related to the Manatee Tempest activity group has been detected. This actor, tracked by Microsoft and known to be a Russia-based cybercriminal group, has been active since June 2014 and is notorious for its Dridex banking trojan campaigns. The group partners with Mustard Tempest to facilitate access to target networks via methods such as drive-by downloads, malvertising, and FakeUpdates infections. They use a BLISTER loader to deploy Cobalt Strike beacons for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. Recently, on host identified by `vnevado-win10s` with the AadDeviceId `f5b847aa-8712-4bf6-b4f7-ed6cd89e1505`, a process with ProcessId `6460` was initiated to execute a command to curl a suspicious URL (`http://vectorsandarrows.com`).

It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

The process `vssblatemp.exe` with process ID 1900 was used to perform the deletion. This incident might be part of a larger malicious campaign as described in the Activity Profile: Iranian MOIS operators opportunistically deploy limited-impact wiper in response to Israel-Hamas war.

SELECT
  DeviceId,
  DeviceName,
  FileName,
  ProcessId,
  ProcessCommandLine,
  TimeGenerated,
  InitiatingProcessFileName,
  InitiatingProcessId,
  InitiatingProcessCommandLine
FROM DeviceProcessEvents
WHERE DeviceId = '1f7d022bfc5cdbb473a0c92dda0343e997c2cd27'
  AND (
    LOWER(FileName) LIKE '%wmi%' OR
    LOWER(ProcessCommandLine) LIKE '%wmi%' OR
    LOWER(InitiatingProcessFileName) LIKE '%wmi%' OR
    LOWER(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) LIKE '%wmi%'
  )
  AND TimeGenerated >= '2024-06-20 09:10:59.878523+00:00'

•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

question.context: The Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on this device, indicating a potential attempt to harvest credentials. Following this, we observed potential lateral movements and ransomware delivery. The incident concluded with a command and control behavior being blocked by our security measures. This signifies an active malware that attempted to establish communication with a remote attacker.
question.question: Can you identify the URL that was associated with the command and control behavior which was blocked?
solution: The Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on host `vnevado-win10v` at `2024-07-04 22:35:00.846286+00:00`.
Lateral movement detected using PSExec to IP address `99.83.111.100` at `2024-07-10 11:24:45.260113+00:00`.
A possible compromised user account `dp5hn` was observed delivering ransomware-related files at `2024-07-04 22:35:01.491898+00:00`.
Command and Control behavior blocked; malware communicating with URL `http://vectorsandarrows.com/` at `2024-07-04 22:35:03.652724+00:00`.

question.context: A suspicious WMI process creation was observed on the machine. Malware frequently uses WMI to spawn new processes, breaking process trees and further infecting a machine. This activity occurred at 2024-07-04 22:35:03.378778+00:00. During the same incident, there was a possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) detected. A PRT is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication and is a JSON Web Token (JWT) issued to enable single sign-on (SSO) across applications used on devices such as Windows 10 and later versions, iOS, and Android. Attackers might attempt to access this token to move laterally or perform credential theft.

trajectory.action:
The telemetry shows that browsercore.exe is indeed directly involved in attempts to access Primary Refresh Tokens and is launched through a suspicious WMI → PowerShell process chain. On multiple hosts, WmiPrvSE.exe (WMI Provider Host) spawns PowerShell, which runs PRT-theft scripts (e.g., get-userprttoken.ps1, humw2135.ps1). These scripts explicitly state that they “get the user’s PRT token from the Azure AD joined or Hybrid joined computer” and “use browsercore.exe to get the PRT token.”

Browsercore.exe is then spawned by these scripts, is repeatedly flagged as suspicious/IOC in alert evidence, and appears with detection metadata and a specific rule ID. The process tree for these detections is:

WmiPrvSE.exe ("wmiprvse.exe -secured -Embedding")
  → powershell.exe ("powershell -File C:\Scripts\get-userprttoken.ps1" or similar PRT tool)
    → browsercore.exe ("browsercore.exe")

This matches the described behavior where malware uses WMI to spawn processes and then targets PRTs for credential theft and lateral movement. Even though the logs we have are from 2024-06-20 and not the 2024-07-04 incident time, they clearly demonstrate that in this environment browsercore.exe is being weaponized as the component that actually interacts with/reads the PRT, under the control of malicious scripts executed via WMI-spawned PowerShell.

Therefore:
- The process browsercore.exe running at the incident time is highly likely to be the process responsible for the PRT access attempt.
- It should be treated as malicious/suspicious in this context, and any browsercore.exe executions spawned by WmiPrvSE → PowerShell should be thoroughly investigated, contained, and hunted for across the environment.

SELECT 
  TimeGenerated,
  DisplayName,
  AlertName,
  AlertSeverity,
  SystemAlertId,
  VendorOriginalId,
  StartTime,
  EndTime,
  Description
FROM SecurityAlert
WHERE 
  LOWER(DisplayName) LIKE '%ransomware%' 
  OR LOWER(AlertName) LIKE '%ransomware%' 
  OR LOWER(Description) LIKE '%ransomware%'
ORDER BY TimeGenerated

trajectory.action:
SELECT 
  TimeGenerated,
  IncidentName,
  Title,
  Severity,
  Status,
  FirstActivityTime,
  LastActivityTime,
  AlertIds
FROM SecurityIncident
ORDER BY TimeGenerated

SELECT 
  sa.SystemAlertId,
  sa.VendorOriginalId,
  sa.StartTime,
  sa.EndTime,
  ae.TimeGenerated AS EvidenceTime,
  ae.DeviceName,
  ae.AccountName,
  ae.AccountUpn,
  ae.FileName,
  ae.ProcessCommandLine
FROM SecurityAlert sa
JOIN AlertEvidence ae
  ON sa.VendorOriginalId = ae.AlertId
WHERE sa.DisplayName LIKE 'Ransomware payload remotely launched%'
ORDER BY sa.EndTime, ae.TimeGenerated

SELECT 
  sa.SystemAlertId,
  sa.VendorOriginalId,
  sa.StartTime,
  sa.EndTime,
  ae.TimeGenerated AS EvidenceTime,
  ae.DeviceName,
  ae.AccountName,
  ae.AccountUpn,
  ae.FileName,
  ae.ProcessCommandLine
FROM SecurityAlert sa
JOIN AlertEvidence ae
  ON ae.AlertId = CONCAT('da', sa.VendorOriginalId)
WHERE sa.DisplayName LIKE 'Ransomware payload remotely launched%'
ORDER BY sa.EndTime DESC, ae.TimeGenerated DESC

[('e34d562e-ef12-4c4e-9bc0-7c6ae357c015', '2024-06-20 09:19:23.690415+00:00', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'High', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

question.question: Related to this alert, there was also an incident where file backups were deleted. Can you identify the command used in the process that deleted the file snapshots and shadow copies?

File backups, including all snapshots and shadow copies, were deleted using process `7236` at `2024-06-20t09:10:51.2193152z` with the command line `vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all`.

question.context: A ransomware payload was remotely launched on a device from the IP address `99.83.111.100`. Attackers might be attempting to encrypt content on this device, rendering it unusable to users. This alert links to suspicious hands-on keyboard user behavior observed on the same device. Suspicious and anomalous user behavior might indicate that a user has been compromised. The end alert indicates that unusual activities, such as changes to the frequency and usage pattern of tools or applications, or the user performing a series of unusual activities, were noticed.

SELECT
    d.InitiatingProcessAccountUpn AS account_upn,
    d.InitiatingProcessAccountName AS account_name,
    d.InitiatingProcessAccountDomain AS account_domain,
    COUNT(DISTINCT d.DeviceName) AS affected_devices,
    COUNT(*) AS file_events
FROM DeviceFileEvents d
JOIN AlertEvidence a
    ON (
        (a.SHA256 IS NOT NULL AND a.SHA256 <> '' AND a.SHA256 = d.SHA256)
        OR (a.SHA1 IS NOT NULL AND a.SHA1 <> '' AND a.SHA1 = d.SHA1)
       )
    AND a.DeviceName = d.DeviceName
WHERE
    (a.ThreatFamily LIKE '%ransom%'
     OR a.Title LIKE '%ransom%'
     OR a.Categories LIKE '%ransom%'
     OR a.AttackTechniques LIKE '%ransom%')
    AND (d.InitiatingProcessAccountUpn IS NOT NULL AND d.InitiatingProcessAccountUpn <> ''
         OR d.InitiatingProcessAccountName IS NOT NULL AND d.InitiatingProcessAccountName <> '')
GROUP BY
    d.InitiatingProcessAccountUpn,
    d.InitiatingProcessAccountName,
    d.InitiatingProcessAccountDomain
ORDER BY
    affected_devices DESC,
    file_events DESC
LIMIT 10

Initial detection included the use of PsExec to launch a command on a remote device, suggesting lateral movement using this tool. This was followed by suspicious activities leading to compromised assets exhibiting ransomware-like behavior. The attacker might be using the specified user account, IP, or device to infect multiple devices with ransomware. Automated remediation actions were considered to address the threat.

There was a lateral movement to the jump server with IP address `99.83.111.100` using PsExec.
A file named `ponceau.7z` is associated with ransomware-like behavior, indicating potentially compromised assets.

This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

('System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

('System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

('System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
